sections.h2: Fastest ways to sell in Downers Grove
sections.html:
Speed points to a direct cash sale in Downers Grove, while a top price points to a broker listing and a house staged for showings. Handling the sale yourself falls in between.

  • A broker suits a house in good shape that can wait through showings and a buyer's loan.
  • Selling alone suits an owner who already knows the local price range.
  • Cash suits estates, houses that need a roof or new systems, occupied rentals and owners relocating on short notice.

At a middle home value of $449,800, each extra month of holding a house means more tax, insurance and utility cost, so the time a direct sale saves deserves a place in your comparison.

If you are weighing the three, start by pricing the work the house needs. Get a roofer, an electrician or a plumber to give a written figure for anything an inspector would flag. Then ask a cash buyer for an offer and an agent for a price opinion on the same house. Subtract commission, repairs, taxes and carrying costs from the listing figure, and compare the result with the cash number.

Downers Grove is a DuPage County village roughly 20 miles from the Chicago Loop, between I-88 and I-55. It has 50,365 residents. Metra's BNSF Line stops three times in the village, at Belmont Road, Main Street and Fairview Avenue, which keeps commuter demand strong. Grade School District 58 runs most of the elementary and middle schools, and Community High School District 99 covers Downers Grove North and South.

Mid-19th-century houses cluster near the center, and every later decade is represented around them. The village has had one of the Chicago area's highest teardown rates, with small older houses replaced by much larger ones. If your house is dated, tell buyers it may suit a rebuild as well as a move-in purchase.

Buyers here often ask about the train, the schools and the age of the mechanicals, so have the answers ready. If the roof, furnace or water heater is near the end of its life, say so plainly and show what you have spent on maintenance. A buyer who plans to tear the house down cares less about finishes and more about the lot, the drainage and the zoning, so tell each type of buyer what matters to them.

Monthly owner costs have a median of $2,553 with a mortgage and $959 without one, which shows what an idle house costs to hold.

Teardowns have been contentious because larger new houses cover more of each lot and push rainwater into neighboring yards and streets. The village's permit page carries its stormwater and tree protection ordinance summaries plus site-management forms such as a construction checklist and a notice to adjacent property owners.

Three practical effects follow for a seller:

  • A buyer planning to rebuild must follow the village's demolition, stormwater and tree rules, so ask Community Development which apply to your lot.
  • Drainage history on your lot matters, so disclose known water problems.
  • Open permits or unfinished work should be closed out before listing.

The permit page also carries residential re-roofing requirements, a contractor list, an encroachment license, a pool information sheet and a form for homeowners acting as their own plumbing contractor. Sellers who made such changes should have their permit paperwork on hand.

The village runs a permit portal through its Customer Self Service system, and its Stormwater Utility and Utility Bill services are separate accounts to settle at sale.

If a buyer wants to demolish, ask them to confirm in the contract that they, not you, will handle any demolition permit and stormwater plan. That keeps village paperwork from landing on your side of the table after closing.

DuPage County collects in arrears, so each year's bill pays for the prior tax year. The Treasurer mails one bill in the spring with two coupons, due around June 1 and September 1.

The general homestead and senior exemptions are each $8,000, and owners should confirm that every exemption they qualify for appears on the bill. A yellow box means a mortgage company is paying, so a second check would be a duplicate. The Treasurer does not set values; the assessor named on your bill answers those questions. Call 630-407-5900 for payment issues.

At closing, your title company can explain how the year's tax is divided. The state's rate under 35 ILCS 200/31-10 is 50 cents per $500 of value or fraction, and the same company can say whether a county or local stamp also applies. For current recording fees, ask the DuPage County Clerk's recording division.

If the bill is paid by your mortgage company, the escrow account may hold a refund after closing, so ask the lender how and when it will be returned. If you pay the bill yourself, keep the receipts for both installments and hand copies to the title company. Missing exemptions are worth checking before you list, because a corrected bill leaves a cleaner proration for both sides.

Preparation prevents surprises at the table.

  1. Find the deed and confirm every name on it will sign.
  2. Print the newest tax bill and see which exemptions it shows.
  3. Ask the village about open permits and finish any unfinished work.
  4. Settle the village utility account before the house changes hands.
  5. Obtain a written payoff from each lender or lienholder.

If you inherited the house, gather the paperwork that shows who may sign early, since a title company will ask for it. List or sell directly, but judge each offer by the net after payoffs, taxes and closing costs, and get terms in writing.

Tell the title company early if the house is held in a trust or by an estate, since extra signatures or documents may be required.

With a cash buyer, the title company searches the record, prepares the deed and collects the transfer tax, and you sign at the closing table. No lender appraisal is needed, so the timeline depends on clean title and how fast payoffs arrive. Ask the buyer in writing who pays title and recording fees, whether the closing date can move if you need extra time to pack, and how the tax bill will be split. Compare the final figure with a listing's net after commission, repairs and carrying costs, not with its asking price.

faqs.q: Which county is Downers Grove in?
faqs.a: DuPage County. Property tax bills come from the DuPage County Treasurer and deeds are recorded with the county.

faqs.q: When do DuPage property taxes fall due?
faqs.a: They are billed a year behind, on one bill with two coupons due around June 1 and September 1.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Downers Grove house to a builder who will tear it down?
faqs.a: Yes. Teardown buyers are common in the village. Share what you know about drainage or trees on the lot, and point them to the village's stormwater, tree protection and demolition requirements.

faqs.q: Which school districts serve Downers Grove?
faqs.a: Most of the village is in Grade School District 58, some areas are in Center Cass District 66, and the two high schools are in Community High School District 99. Check your tax bill to see which districts your parcel pays.

faqs.q: How can I avoid paying my tax bill twice?
faqs.a: Check for the yellow box on your bill. It shows when a mortgage company is paying, and in that case you should not send another payment.
